newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: NEW STRIKE THREATENS HUNTER VALLEY COAL EXPORTS.
newsitem.headline: NEW STRIKE THREATENS HUNTER VALLEY COAL EXPORTS.

text.p: Mining giant Rio Tinto Ltd on Monday was bracing itself for another strike at its Hunter Valley No 1 coking and thermal coal mine north of Sydney.
Mine management and delegates from the Construction, Forestry Mining and Energy Union (CFMEU) on Monday morning were locked in last-minute talks.
A spokesman for mine owner Coal and Allied Industries Ltd (CAIL), owned about 70 percent by Rio Tinto, told Reuters that it remained unclear whether the workers would strike.
CFMEU officials were not immediately available for comment.

The union has, however, served notice on CAIL that a new strike will begin on Tuesday morning, three weeks after the end of a cooling-off period which began after the last six-week strike, on July 22.

Hunter Valley No 1 normally produces about 25,000 tonnes of coal a day. The last strike cost the group about one million tonnes of coal, or about A$40 million in lost sales revenue, over 40 days. CAIL supplies Japanese and other east Asian power stations, steel mills and industrial customers with semi-soft coking coal and thermal coal.

Sticking points in the current talks involve management dissatisfaction over work practices. The CFMEU has voiced dissatisfaction with management wishes to use non-unionised staff, introduce individual employment contracts and use state government trains to ship coal in the event of a strike.
A CAIL spokesman said the company had presented two collective agreement offers to the union, as requested.
The union had rejected both and continued to complain about the non-issue of individual employment contracts, he said.
Work practices which the company was not satisfied with partly stemmed from union control over mine hiring and firing, overtime and shift allocation, he said.

CAIL wanted the mine to operate on continuous production. It also wanted an end to all union demarcation, so that flexible work practices coild be introduced, as well as employment and shift allocation conducted on merit, he said.

CAIL officials said after the end of the last strike that exports had been maintained through that strike through shipments from stockpiles, which were partly supplied by other group mines in the region.
The strike-prone mine has a capital value of A$430 million, a fact sheet issued by CAIL showed.
The average salary of truck drivers at the mine is A$73,000 to A$83,000 a year for a 42.5 hour week. Salary was A$97,000 a year with overtime and other benefits.
